title: The Case of the Fourteen Hundred Missing Books
story: The stocktake says the library holds fourteen hundred fewer books than the catalogue claims, and four explanations are already in circulation. All four describe something that genuinely happened. The loans system lists sixty books out past their due date, which is sixty books and not fourteen hundred. A shelf survey found forty-one books filed in the wrong room, and a book in the wrong room is still in the building. The theft log records about fifteen losses a year for the last three years, which comes to forty-five. One shelf was counted twice during the stocktake, which flatters the count by thirty and makes the gap look smaller, not larger. Those four together account for a hundred and forty-six books at the very most. During the refit in August a contractor cleared the two bays of withdrawn stock into a skip. Nobody marked those books as withdrawn in the catalogue, because marking them was the librarian's job and she was on leave. The two bays held between six and seven hundred books on each of their eleven shelves. That is the only event in the year that is the right size to explain the gap.
question: Where did fourteen hundred books go?

suspects.why: a contractor cleared two bays of withdrawn stock into a skip and nobody marked them as withdrawn
the loans system lists sixty books out past their due date, which is sixty books and not fourteen hundred
a shelf survey found forty-one books filed in the wrong room, and a book in the wrong room is still in the building
the theft log records about fifteen losses a year for the last three years, which comes to forty-five
one shelf was counted twice, which flatters the count by thirty and makes the gap look smaller, not larger

answer: The withdrawn stock went into a skip and was never taken off the catalogue.
proof: “Those four together account for a hundred and forty-six books at the very most.”
“The two bays held between six and seven hundred books on each of their eleven shelves.”
“That is the only event in the year that is the right size to explain the gap.”
clears: Overdue loans: “sixty books and not fourteen hundred.”
Misshelving: “a book in the wrong room is still in the building.”
Theft: “about fifteen losses a year for the last three years, which comes to forty-five.”
The double count: “makes the gap look smaller, not larger.”
explain: Nobody in this case is lying. Books are overdue, books are misshelved, books are stolen, and the count has a flaw in it. Add every one of them at its worst and you are still twelve hundred short. Only the skip is the right order of magnitude, and the reason it was never suspected is that it was paperwork rather than a loss.

title: The Case of the Bread Order That Doubled
story: The kitchen's bread order has gone from ninety loaves a week to a hundred and fifty, and the business manager wants to know who is eating it. Four answers have been offered and all four are true as far as they go. Twelve pupils joined in September, and twelve pupils eat about four loaves a week between them. The new sandwich option sells forty rounds a day, which the kitchen measured at twenty-seven loaves a week. The waste bin was weighed every day for a fortnight and threw away the equivalent of three loaves. The price per loaf fell in August, which changes the bill and not the number of loaves. Those three real increases come to thirty-four loaves, and the order has risen by sixty. The supplier changed its standard loaf in August from eight hundred grams to four hundred. Ninety of the old loaves was seventy-two kilograms of bread, and a hundred and fifty of the new ones is sixty. The kitchen is baking into more loaves and less bread than it was last year.
question: Why has the bread order risen by sixty loaves?

suspects.why: the supplier changed its standard loaf in August from eight hundred grams to four hundred
twelve pupils joined in September, and twelve pupils eat about four loaves a week between them
the new sandwich option sells forty rounds a day, which the kitchen measured at twenty-seven loaves a week
the waste bin was weighed every day for a fortnight and threw away the equivalent of three loaves
the price per loaf fell in August, which changes the bill and not the number of loaves

answer: The supplier halved the loaf, so the same bread needs twice the loaves.
proof: “Those three real increases come to thirty-four loaves, and the order has risen by sixty.”
“Ninety of the old loaves was seventy-two kilograms of bread, and a hundred and fifty of the new ones is sixty.”
“The kitchen is baking into more loaves and less bread than it was last year.”
clears: New pupils: “twelve pupils eat about four loaves a week between them.”
The sandwich option: “twenty-seven loaves a week.”
Waste: “threw away the equivalent of three loaves.”
The price: “changes the bill and not the number of loaves.”
explain: Three of the suspects really are adding loaves, and together they add thirty-four of the sixty. The last thirty come from the unit, not from anybody's appetite. Weigh the order instead of counting it and the mystery reverses: the school is eating twelve kilograms less bread than it was a year ago.

title: The Case of the Pencils That Vanished Three Times Faster
story: The stock cupboard issued nine hundred pencils last year and three thousand this year, for a school that has barely changed size. Four reasons have been put forward, and none of them is invented. Forty more pupils joined, which is seven percent of six hundred, or about sixty-three pencils at last year's rate. Breakages were counted for a fortnight and ran at four a day, which is roughly a hundred and fifty over a year. Pupils do take pencils home, and a sample of thirty bags on one afternoon turned up eleven. The cupboard now issues by the box of twelve rather than singly, which changes how pencils leave the shelf but not how fast they are used up. Those four together cannot reach three hundred. The electric sharpener was installed in September beside the cupboard. A hand sharpener takes about a millimetre off a pencil and the electric one takes four before it stops. A pencil that used to last nine weeks now lasts three. Three times the consumption on nine hundred is twenty-seven hundred, and twenty-seven hundred is the gap.
question: Why did pencil use triple?

suspects.why: a hand sharpener takes about a millimetre off a pencil and the electric one takes four before it stops
forty more pupils is seven percent of six hundred, or about sixty-three pencils at last year's rate
breakages were counted for a fortnight and ran at four a day, which is roughly a hundred and fifty over a year
a sample of thirty bags on one afternoon turned up eleven
issuing by the box changes how pencils leave the shelf but not how fast they are used up

answer: The electric sharpener eats four times as much pencil per sharpening.
proof: “Those four together cannot reach three hundred.”
“A pencil that used to last nine weeks now lasts three.”
“Three times the consumption on nine hundred is twenty-seven hundred, and twenty-seven hundred is the gap.”
clears: More pupils: “about sixty-three pencils at last year's rate.”
Breakages: “roughly a hundred and fifty over a year.”
Taken home: “a sample of thirty bags on one afternoon turned up eleven.”
Issuing by the box: “changes how pencils leave the shelf but not how fast they are used up.”
explain: Growth, breakage and pilfering are all real and all small, and the box system moves pencils without consuming them. The sharpener is the only suspect that multiplies rather than adds, and multiplying is what a threefold rise needs. Four millimetres a sharpening is nothing to watch and everything to the total.

title: The Case of the Orchard That Lost Three Quarters
story: The school orchard picked four hundred kilograms last autumn and ninety this one, and four causes have been proposed by four different people. Each of them is genuinely at work in that orchard. The neighbour's new hedge shades two of the eleven trees, so at the very worst it can cost two elevenths of the crop. Wasp damage was counted on a sample of two hundred apples and came to five percent. The trees have not been pruned for three years, which the county guide says costs about fifteen percent of a yield. Apples crop heavily one year and lightly the next, which can halve a harvest on its own. Put every one of those at its maximum and you still have well over a hundred and fifty kilograms. The weather station logged minus three degrees on the night of the twenty-second of April. The trees were in full flower that night, and a frost at full flower kills the flowers outright. No flower means no fruit at all from that tree, not a reduced crop. The two trees against the south wall flower a week later than the rest, and they carried most of the ninety kilograms.
question: What took three quarters of the crop?

suspects.why: the weather station logged minus three degrees on the night of the twenty-second of April, when the trees were in full flower
the hedge shades two of the eleven trees, so at the very worst it can cost two elevenths of the crop
wasp damage was counted on a sample of two hundred apples and came to five percent
the county guide says three years without pruning costs about fifteen percent of a yield
apples crop heavily one year and lightly the next, which can halve a harvest on its own

answer: A frost on the night of the twenty-second killed the blossom.
proof: “Put every one of those at its maximum and you still have well over a hundred and fifty kilograms.”
“No flower means no fruit at all from that tree, not a reduced crop.”
“The two trees against the south wall flower a week later than the rest, and they carried most of the ninety kilograms.”
clears: The hedge: “at the very worst it can cost two elevenths of the crop.”
Wasps: “came to five percent.”
No pruning: “costs about fifteen percent of a yield.”
Biennial cropping: “which can halve a harvest on its own.”
explain: Four real reductions, stacked at their worst, still leave more than a hundred and fifty kilograms on the trees. Only the frost works by subtraction to zero rather than by percentage, and the two late-flowering trees prove it: they missed the cold night and they carried the harvest.

title: The Case of the Ride That Took Thirteen Minutes Longer
story: Noor's five-kilometre ride to school has gone from eighteen minutes to thirty-one, and she has four theories, all of them founded on something real. The new traffic lights at the bridge were timed over a week and cost her an average of forty seconds. Her rear tyre is soft, and the cycling club's own figures put a soft tyre at about a minute over five kilometres. The roadworks detour was measured on the map at six hundred extra metres, which is two minutes at her speed. There has been a headwind most mornings this month, worth perhaps a minute on an exposed road. Those four add up to four and a half minutes against a loss of thirteen. The rear brake was adjusted in March and the pad has sat against the rim ever since. A wheel lifted off the ground and spun by hand stops in two seconds, where a free wheel spins for forty. A brake that never lets go is working against her for every metre of the ride, uphill, downhill and flat. Nothing else in the list is still costing her anything once she is past it.
question: What is taking the extra time?

suspects.why: the rear brake was adjusted in March and the pad has sat against the rim ever since
the new traffic lights at the bridge were timed over a week and cost her an average of forty seconds
the cycling club's own figures put a soft tyre at about a minute over five kilometres
the detour was measured on the map at six hundred extra metres, which is two minutes at her speed
there has been a headwind most mornings this month, worth perhaps a minute on an exposed road

answer: A brake pad has been dragging on the rim since March.
proof: “Those four add up to four and a half minutes against a loss of thirteen.”
“A wheel lifted off the ground and spun by hand stops in two seconds, where a free wheel spins for forty.”
“A brake that never lets go is working against her for every metre of the ride, uphill, downhill and flat.”
clears: The lights: “cost her an average of forty seconds.”
The tyre: “about a minute over five kilometres.”
The detour: “which is two minutes at her speed.”
The wind: “worth perhaps a minute on an exposed road.”
explain: Four honest delays, four and a half minutes between them. The brake is different in kind as well as in size, because the others take their toll at one place or in one condition and the brake takes its toll continuously. The spin test turns that into a number anybody can check in ten seconds.

title: The Case of the Nine Missing Litres
story: The ninety-litre class tank drops nine litres a week, and the log carries four suggestions from four different weeks. Every one of them loses some water. An open bowl of the same surface area was left beside the tank as a test and evaporated one point two litres in seven days. The filter outlet does splash, but the shelf and the floor under it were dry every morning for a fortnight. Gravel and ornaments were topped up in September and hold water, though a one-off absorption cannot repeat itself every week. The fish were blamed in October, and eleven small fish displace water rather than consuming it. Together those come to under two litres, and seven are unaccounted for. The hose from the external filter weeps where it joins the canister inside the cabinet. The towel under that joint weighs one point one kilograms dry and two point four when it is changed each morning. That is one point three litres a day, which is nine litres a week. The cabinet was not opened at all between September and the week the towel was found.
question: Where are the nine litres going?

suspects.why: the hose from the external filter weeps where it joins the canister inside the cabinet
an open bowl of the same surface area evaporated one point two litres in seven days
the filter outlet does splash, but the shelf and the floor under it were dry every morning for a fortnight
a one-off absorption cannot repeat itself every week
eleven small fish displace water rather than consuming it

answer: A weeping hose joint inside the cabinet loses over a litre a day.
proof: “Together those come to under two litres, and seven are unaccounted for.”
“The towel under that joint weighs one point one kilograms dry and two point four when it is changed each morning.”
“That is one point three litres a day, which is nine litres a week.”
clears: Evaporation: “evaporated one point two litres in seven days.”
Splashing: “the shelf and the floor under it were dry every morning for a fortnight.”
The gravel: “a one-off absorption cannot repeat itself every week.”
The fish: “displace water rather than consuming it.”
explain: Evaporation is real and it is one and a bit litres. Everything else on the list is either zero or cannot happen twice. The towel is the whole case: weigh it wet, weigh it dry, and the difference is a measurement of the leak rather than an opinion about it.

title: The Case of the Hall That Got Twelve Decibels Louder
story: Assembly measured sixty-six decibels last year and seventy-eight this year, and four changes have been offered to explain it. All four happened. Thirty more children come to assembly, and sound adds on a scale where doubling a crowd buys you three decibels, so thirty more on three hundred is under half of one. The new public address system was measured at seventy decibels a metre from the speaker, which is what the old one gave. The ceiling fan was tested alone in an empty hall and read fifty-one, which is below the level of the room before anybody speaks. The chairs were replaced with plastic ones that squeak, and a squeak is brief and sharp rather than a rise in the whole level. The refit took out the full-length curtains and the carpet at the back and put down a hard floor. Reverberation time in the empty hall has gone from nought point nine seconds to two point six. In a room that holds its sound for nearly three seconds, every voice is still arriving while the next one starts. Nothing in the hall is making more noise than it did; the hall has stopped absorbing it.

title: The Case of the Drain That Everyone Blamed on Leaves
story: The yard floods to a depth of ten centimetres in any heavy rain, and leaves have been blamed for three autumns. The gully was rodded and cleared the morning before the last storm and the yard flooded anyway. The gutter guards were fitted in September and the gutters were found clear afterwards. The sycamores do drop about twenty-five kilograms of litter each, which is a genuine nuisance and a slow one. The drain itself is a hundred millimetre pipe, and the manufacturer rates it at two thousand litres an hour. Thirty millimetres of rain fell in that hour onto the original roof, which measures three hundred square metres. Three hundred square metres taking thirty millimetres is nine thousand litres in one hour. The new sports hall roof was finished in July and plumbed into the same downpipe. It adds a hundred and eighty square metres, which is another five thousand four hundred litres in the same hour. A pipe rated for two thousand litres is being asked to take fourteen thousand. Clearing leaves out of a pipe does not make the pipe any wider.

the gully was rodded and cleared the morning before the last storm and the yard flooded anyway

the gutter guards were fitted in September and the gutters were found clear afterwards
thirty millimetres of rain fell in that hour onto the original roof, which measures three hundred square metres

“A pipe rated for two thousand litres is being asked to take fourteen thousand.”
“Clearing leaves out of a pipe does not make the pipe any wider.”
clears: Leaves in the gully: “the gully was rodded and cleared the morning before the last storm and the yard flooded anyway.”

The storm is real and the old roof alone already overran the pipe by four and a half times. The extra roof is what turned an occasional overflow into every heavy rain, and no amount of sweeping addresses it.

title: The Case of the Pumpkin That Stopped Growing
story: The competition pumpkin reached sixty kilograms when the seed packet promises two hundred, and four growers have offered four reasons. None of them is nonsense. It was given ninety litres of water a day against a recommended eighty, and too much water swells a fruit rather than starving it. A soil test in June came back normal for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. It was pollinated on the eleventh of June, which is four days later than ideal and costs perhaps a week of growing. The patch gets six hours of direct sun where the guide asks for eight, which is a real shortfall of a quarter. Taken together those might take fifty kilograms off a record, and a hundred and forty are missing. The main vine was cut through by a mower on the twenty-ninth of July, forty days in. A pumpkin is fed by its leaves and everything they make travels to the fruit along that one vine. Before the cut it was drawing on about four hundred leaves and afterwards on the six beyond the break. The fruit measured eleven kilograms a day in July and under one kilogram a day in August.
question: Why did the pumpkin stop at sixty kilograms?

it was given ninety litres a day against a recommended eighty, and too much water swells a fruit rather than starving it
a soil test in June came back normal for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
it was pollinated four days later than ideal, which costs perhaps a week of growing
the patch gets six hours of direct sun where the guide asks for eight, which is a real shortfall of a quarter

answer: A mower cut the vine and left the fruit with six leaves instead of four hundred.

“Before the cut it was drawing on about four hundred leaves and afterwards on the six beyond the break.”
“The fruit measured eleven kilograms a day in July and under one kilogram a day in August.”
clears: Too much water: “swells a fruit rather than starving it.”
The soil: “came back normal for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.”
Late pollination: “costs perhaps a week of growing.”
Too little sun: “a real shortfall of a quarter.”

title: The Case of the Four Kilograms of Mud

The football pitch is the obvious culprit, except that boots are changed in the boot room and the mat there was weighed at four hundred grams a day. The reception children's garden is wet, but reception has its own door at the far end and its own corridor. Those four together were measured over a week at under seven hundred grams a day. In October a shortcut appeared across the field, and the grass along it is worn to bare soil for forty metres. A count on three mornings found a hundred and eighty children using it. Twenty grams on a shoe is a smear nobody would notice, and a hundred and eighty of them is three point six kilograms.

title: The Case of the Fuel Bill That Rose a Third
story: The minibus burned two thousand six hundred litres last spring and three thousand four hundred this spring, and four reasons have been put forward by the office. Each describes something that really changed. Fuel went up nine percent a litre in October, which raises the bill and leaves the litres exactly where they were. The route was altered in November and the new one is one point two kilometres longer on twenty-six, which is five percent. The driver's log shows an average of twelve minutes idling at the depot each day, worth about three percent of the fuel. The tyres were found twenty percent under pressure in February, which the manufacturer puts at three percent on consumption. Added together those changes account for eleven percent, and the rise is thirty-one. The second minibus failed its test in September and has been off the road since. This bus has covered the other route as well on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Fridays. The odometer reads nine thousand four hundred kilometres last spring and twelve thousand two hundred this spring. Thirty percent more distance in a vehicle that has not otherwise changed burns thirty percent more fuel.

an average of twelve minutes idling each day is worth about three percent of the fuel
the tyres were twenty percent under pressure, which the manufacturer puts at three percent on consumption

The route: “one point two kilometres longer on twenty-six, which is five percent.”

title: The Case of the Sports Fund That Was Eighteen Hundred Short
story: The sports fund should hold two thousand four hundred pounds and the statement shows five hundred and sixty. Four explanations are on the table and each one is a genuine outgoing. The engraving on the county trophy cost a hundred and ten pounds, and the invoice is in the folder. Unpaid subscriptions come to ninety-five pounds, which is money that never arrived rather than money that left. Bank charges run at three pounds a month, which is thirty-six pounds across the year. The cash tin float was raised from twenty pounds to fifty in September, moving thirty pounds rather than spending it. Those four come to two hundred and seventy-one pounds at the very most, and the hole is eighteen hundred and forty. The kit order was placed by the office in June and placed again by the coach in July. Both orders were paid, and the supplier's statement shows two payments of nine hundred and twenty pounds eleven days apart. One delivery was signed for and the second was never chased, because nobody knew to expect it. Eighteen hundred and forty pounds is exactly two times nine hundred and twenty.

title: The Case of the Eight Degrees Lost Overnight

The loft hatch above the stairs was left open, which the same survey put at half a degree. Those four together come to about three degrees against a fall of eight. The boiler fault log shows a lockout at ten past eleven and no firing at all until the caretaker reset it at half past six. title: The Case of the Two Kilograms of Seed a Day
story: The feeders on the field are emptying two kilograms of seed a day, and four eaters have been blamed by the four people who watch them. All four are genuinely eating from them. The catch tray underneath was emptied and weighed for a week and held sixty grams of spilled seed a day. The finches come in ones and twos and eat about the same as a sparrow. Those four together are under four hundred grams of the two thousand. The pigeons arrive at half past three, after the watchers have gone home, and the caretaker counted forty on and under the feeders. A woodpigeon eats about forty grams of grain a day, and forty of them is sixteen hundred grams. The birds that are seen all day are the ones that eat least.

title: The Case of the Urn That Took Forty Minutes
story: The staff room urn used to boil in twelve minutes and now takes forty, and four explanations have been offered. Each one slows a boil. It is filled to eighteen litres now rather than seventeen, which is six percent more water and about forty seconds. The staff room has been two degrees colder since the radiator valve stuck, which costs under a minute from a cold start. The lid is often left off, and a test with the lid on and off put the difference at six minutes. There is about a millimetre of limescale on the elements, which the manual says adds roughly five percent to a boiling time. Those four together account for eight minutes of the twenty-eight that have been added. The urn has three heating elements and an engineer measured the resistance across all three in February. Two of them are open circuit and have been since the power surge in January. One element doing the work of three takes three times as long to deliver the same heat. Twelve minutes multiplied by three is thirty-six, and the other faults account for the rest.

eighteen litres rather than seventeen is six percent more water and about forty seconds

a test with the lid on and off put the difference at six minutes
about a millimetre of limescale adds roughly five percent to a boiling time

proof: “Those four together account for eight minutes of the twenty-eight that have been added.”
“One element doing the work of three takes three times as long to deliver the same heat.”
“Twelve minutes multiplied by three is thirty-six, and the other faults account for the rest.”

The lid: “put the difference at six minutes.”

title: The Case of the Hundred Cards That Never Arrived

title: The Case of the Eruption That Reached Thirty Centimetres
story: The model volcano threw its foam thirty centimetres and the club record is two metres, and four differences have been proposed. All four are real differences from the record attempt. The bottle neck is thirty-five millimetres across where the record used twenty, and a wider neck does let the foam out more slowly. Forty grams of bicarbonate was used against the record's sixty, which is a third less gas. The vinegar is five percent acid and the record used eight, which is another real shortfall. The room was four degrees cooler, which slows a reaction a little without changing how much gas it makes. Those four might halve a height between them, and this one is down by six sevenths. The record attempt adds ten millilitres of washing-up liquid and this one used none. Gas on its own rises through the liquid and bursts at the surface, so most of it never lifts anything. title: The Case of the Jewels That Fell Off the Crown
story: Thirty-eight of the forty stones on the play's crown were on the floor by the end of the first rehearsal, and four reasons have been offered. All four are true of that crown. title: The Case of the Stage That Sagged Eleven Millimetres
story: The stage floor dips eleven millimetres under the piano and the builder's limit is three. Four loads have been blamed and every one of them is really up there. The piano weighs four hundred and eighty kilograms on four castors, which is a heavy point load and the obvious suspect. The choir of forty stands on the same stage, and forty people at sixty kilograms is two thousand four hundred kilograms. The staging blocks at the back add another hundred and ten. The lighting bar is hung from the ceiling and carries none of its weight on the floor at all. The stage was built for a distributed load four times what it now carries, and it did not sag last year under the same choir. A cable run was cut through the main joist in two thousand and nineteen, taking its depth from two hundred and twenty millimetres to ninety. The stiffness of a joist goes with the cube of its depth, not with the depth itself. Ninety cubed against two hundred and twenty cubed leaves about seven percent of the original stiffness. title: The Case of the String That Weighed More Than the Kite
story: The kite flew well on the first day and will not leave the ground now, and four additions have been blamed. Every one of them is extra weight that was not there on the first day. title: The Case of the Seeds That Did Not Come Up
story: Eleven seedlings came up from a tray of two hundred seeds and four reasons have been given, all of them genuine faults in the sowing. The packet is dated last March, and the seed house puts the fall in germination at about ten percent a year. The compost was the cheap bag left over from last summer, which the trial tray showed is worth perhaps another ten percent. The windowsill held at fourteen degrees where the packet asks for eighteen, which slows germination and does not stop it. The tray was watered once a week rather than kept damp, which the same trial put at fifteen percent. Those four at their worst would still leave well over a hundred seedlings. The seed was pressed in with a thumb to a depth of about two centimetres. The packet asks for five millimetres and says in bold that the seed needs light to germinate. A seed buried four times too deep in the dark never starts at all, whatever the compost or the temperature. A second tray from the same packet, sown at five millimetres into the same cheap compost, gave a hundred and sixty-eight.

title: The Case of the Eggs That Stopped in October
story: The six hens laid twenty-eight eggs a week in July and nine a week in late October, and four causes have been suggested. All four are at work in that run. Two of the hens are moulting, and a moulting hen stops laying for a few weeks, which accounts for perhaps eight eggs. The nights have turned cold, and the poultry guide puts a modest drop on cold without calling it a main cause. A fox got into the garden in September and frightened the birds, which costs a few days of laying rather than a season. The feed was changed in August to a brand with the same protein figure printed on the sack. Those four together might explain ten or eleven of the nineteen eggs that have gone. Daylight in the run has fallen from sixteen hours in July to nine hours now. The guide is blunt about it: laying falls away sharply below twelve hours and stops near nine. Light reaching the eye is what tells a hen the season, and nothing about the sack of feed changes that. The neighbour's flock under a lamp on a timer is still laying at July's rate.

title: The Case of the Beans That Died in the Experiment
story: All twenty-four bean plants in the growth experiment died in eleven days and four causes have been written up. Each is a real departure from the method. The bench ran at twenty-six degrees where the method asks for twenty-two, which the control group shows costs growth and does not kill. The pots are seven centimetres where the method specifies nine, which crowds a root system at four weeks and not at eleven days. They were watered on alternate days rather than daily, and the control tray on the same watering is alive. The lamp sat fifty centimetres above the plants rather than thirty, which weakens a seedling over weeks. Those four together describe a slow decline and not a total loss inside a fortnight. The liquid feed was made up at five millilitres into five hundred millilitres of water. The label says five millilitres into five litres, so the solution is ten times the strength intended. A feed at ten times strength pulls water back out of the roots instead of giving anything to them. The control tray, fed from a bottle mixed by the technician, is forty centimetres tall.

the control tray on the same watering is alive

title: The Case of the Ice Cream That Served Fourteen

title: The Case of the Cylinder That Filled Ninety Balloons
story: The helium cylinder is labelled for four hundred and fifty balloons and it filled ninety. Four causes have been suggested and each wastes some gas. The nozzle hisses when the balloon is pulled off, and a timed test put that at about two percent of the cylinder. The label's figure assumes a balloon blown to twenty-three centimetres across, which is the size printed on the packet. The ones filled on the day measured thirty-eight centimetres, because a bigger balloon looked better. Volume goes with the cube of the width, and thirty-eight divided by twenty-three, cubed, is about four and a half. Four hundred and fifty divided by four and a half is a hundred, and the wasted gas accounts for the last ten.
